body:
WIPO and WTO perform different functions

The World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) is an international organisation concerned with intellectual property cooperation, treaties and services. The convention establishing WIPO was signed in 1967, entered into force in 1970, and WIPO became a specialised agency of the United Nations in 1974.

WIPO administers important IP treaties and provides international filing and registration services. The World Trade Organization (WTO), in contrast, administers the TRIPS Agreement as part of the multilateral trading system. WTO members' obligations under TRIPS are subject to the WTO's applicable dispute-settlement framework.

WIPO is associated with IP treaties, cooperation and international filing services. WTO is associated with the trade-related legal obligations of TRIPS. Neither organisation automatically grants a patent enforceable in every country.

Important treaties administered by WIPO

TreatyYearCore purpose
Paris Convention1883Protection of industrial property, including national treatment and priority rights
Berne Convention1886International protection of literary and artistic works, including protection without registration formalities as a condition
Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT)1970Common international patent-application procedure
Madrid Protocol1989International system for seeking trademark protection in designated members
WIPO Copyright Treaty (WCT)1996Copyright protection, including issues arising in the digital environment
WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty (WPPT)1996International protection concerning performers and producers of phonograms

The Paris Convention and priority rights

The Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property provides an important right of priority. A person who files a qualifying first application in one contracting country may, within the relevant period, file corresponding applications in other contracting countries and claim the priority of the first filing.

The ordinary priority period is 12 months for patents and utility models and 6 months for trademarks and industrial designs. Claiming priority does not itself mean the applicant has obtained protection everywhere. An application must still meet the requirements of the country or system in which protection is sought.

The PCT does not grant a world patent

The Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) allows an applicant to seek patent protection in multiple countries through a common international application procedure. The process generally involves an international filing and search, followed by proceedings before the relevant national or regional offices.

The PCT simplifies aspects of seeking protection abroad, but decisions about patent grant remain with the relevant national or regional patent authorities. An international application is therefore not a worldwide patent grant.

Trademark and copyright arrangements

The Madrid Protocol facilitates seeking protection for a trademark in multiple designated members through an international registration system. The designated members retain powers under the applicable rules to refuse protection in their territories. Madrid registration must not be confused with a trademark that is automatically valid everywhere.

The Berne Convention is a central international agreement for copyright. Its protection-without-formalities principle means that copyright protection under the Convention is not conditional on compulsory registration. The WCT and WPPT subsequently addressed additional copyright and related-rights issues, including those arising from digital technologies.

India's participation in selected WIPO treaties

Important dates recorded by WIPO for India include the entry into force of both the Paris Convention and PCT on 7 December 1998, the Madrid Protocol on 8 July 2013, and the WCT and WPPT on 25 December 2018. These are dates on which the treaties became effective for India, not the dates on which the original treaties were concluded.

Development concerns and national policy

IP policy involves choices about innovation incentives, competition, access to knowledge, research collaboration and the needs of developing economies. WIPO adopted its Development Agenda in 2007 to integrate development considerations into its work.

India's National Intellectual Property Rights Policy was approved by the Union Cabinet on 12 May 2016. It provides an overall policy framework for awareness, creation, management, protection, enforcement and commercialisation of IP. It does not replace the Patents Act or other IP statutes, and it does not eliminate the public-interest provisions available under Indian law.

For Gujarat, national patent rules apply alongside practical support provided by institutions such as the Gujarat Council on Science and Technology's Intellectual Property Facilitation Centre at Gandhinagar. Innovators therefore operate within a combination of national law, international obligations and local institutional support.

Connecting the full subtopic

Intellectual property can support innovation by allowing its owner to control specified uses and obtain commercial returns. Assignment transfers ownership, whereas voluntary licensing allows another party to use protected technology within agreed limits. Universities and research institutions can use these arrangements to connect inventions with industry and society.

When important technology is unavailable or unaffordable, public-interest rules may permit specified intervention, including compulsory licensing under domestic legal conditions. For technologies required by standards, SEP licensing and FRAND commitments can influence access and competition. Internationally, WTO TRIPS sets minimum obligations and recognises flexibilities, while WIPO treaties and systems facilitate cooperation and applications for protection across countries.

Prelims focus

  • WIPO was established under a 1967 convention and became a UN specialised agency in 1974.
  • Paris Convention: 1883; priority periods are 12 months for patents and 6 months for trademarks and designs.
  • PCT: 1970; it provides an international application procedure, not an international patent grant.
  • Madrid Protocol: 1989; it concerns trademarks.
  • WCT and WPPT: 1996; both became effective for India on 25 December 2018.
  • India approved its National IPR Policy on 12 May 2016.
  • Trap: WIPO administers IP treaties and services, but TRIPS belongs to the WTO framework.

[Sources: WIPO, Summary of the Convention Establishing WIPO, 1967, and WIPO History, consulted 14 November 2026; WIPO, Summary of the Paris Convention, section on right of priority; WIPO, PCT Frequently Asked Questions, updated August 2026, section on international filing and national-phase decisions; WIPO, treaty summaries for the Berne Convention, Madrid Protocol, WCT and WPPT; WIPO Lex, India, WIPO-Administered Treaties, entry-into-force dates, consulted 14 November 2026; WIPO, Development Agenda history; Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, Government of India, National Intellectual Property Rights Policy, approved 12 May 2016; GUJCOST, Intellectual Property Facilitation Centre, consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The PCT, concluded in 1970, provides a shared filing and search pathway, followed by separate national or regional grant decisions; it issues no worldwide patent.
pictures.caption: One PCT application can lead to separate national or regional patent decisions.

pictures.alt: IP ownership branches into assignment and voluntary licensing, alongside special licensing situations, international frameworks and Indian support.
pictures.caption: Intellectual property connects innovation, licensing, public interest and international rules.

title: WIPO Treaties, International Filing Systems and India's IP Policy
